notes.definition: One theory suggests that during the first billion years of the Earth's existence, intense volcanic activity released gases that formed the early atmosphere, which was mainly carbon dioxide with little or no oxygen, and water vapour that condensed to form the oceans.
explanation: Theories about what was in the Earth's early atmosphere, and how it was formed, have changed and developed over time. Evidence for the early atmosphere is limited because of the very long time scale involved: the Earth is about 4.6 billion years old. There were no people to measure the gases, and very little rock from that time survives unchanged, so scientists have to use indirect evidence and models.

One theory is that during the first billion years of the Earth's existence there was intense volcanic activity. The volcanoes released gases that formed the early atmosphere. They also released water vapour. As the Earth cooled, this water vapour condensed to form the oceans.

At the start of this period the Earth's atmosphere may have been like the atmospheres of Mars and Venus today. These consist mainly of carbon dioxide with little or no oxygen gas. Volcanoes also produced nitrogen, which gradually built up in the atmosphere. There may also have been small proportions of methane (CH₄) and ammonia (NH₃).

When the oceans formed, carbon dioxide dissolved in the water. Carbonates were then precipitated, producing sediments on the sea bed. This reduced the amount of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere. Later, living organisms changed the atmosphere further (see how oxygen increased and how carbon dioxide decreased).

In the exam you may be given information about a theory and asked to interpret the evidence or evaluate it. Good evaluation points include: whether the evidence supports the theory, how reliable the evidence is (it is indirect and limited because of the time scale), whether there is other evidence that agrees (such as gases released by volcanoes today, and the atmospheres of Mars and Venus), and why scientists cannot be certain.
keyFacts: The Earth is about 4.6 billion years old.
Evidence for the early atmosphere is limited because of the long time scale.
In the first billion years, intense volcanic activity released gases that formed the early atmosphere.
Volcanoes released water vapour, which condensed to form the oceans as the Earth cooled.
The early atmosphere was probably mainly carbon dioxide, with little or no oxygen, like Mars and Venus today.
Volcanoes also produced nitrogen, which gradually built up in the atmosphere.
There may have been small proportions of methane and ammonia.
Carbon dioxide dissolved in the oceans and carbonates precipitated as sediments, reducing atmospheric carbon dioxide.

keyTerms.definition: The gases surrounding the Earth during roughly its first billion years, thought to be mainly carbon dioxide with little or no oxygen.
Eruptions of volcanoes, which release gases such as carbon dioxide, water vapour and nitrogen.
Change state from a gas to a liquid when cooled, as water vapour did to form the oceans.
An insoluble solid formed in a solution; carbonates precipitated from the oceans to form sediments.
Solid material that settles to the bottom of a liquid, such as the sea bed, and can later form rock.
A scientific explanation supported by evidence, which can change as new evidence is found.

workedExamples.title: Comparing the composition of Mars with Earth today
workedExamples.question: The atmosphere of Mars is about 95% carbon dioxide. The Earth's atmosphere today is about 0.04% carbon dioxide. How many times greater is the percentage of carbon dioxide on Mars?
steps: Divide the larger percentage by the smaller one: 95 ÷ 0.04.
workedExamples.answer: About 2400 times greater (2375). This supports the idea that an atmosphere made by volcanoes, without life, is mainly carbon dioxide.

workedExamples.title: Using a fraction of geological time
workedExamples.question: Intense volcanic activity happened during the first billion years of the Earth's 4.6 billion year history. Calculate this as a percentage of the Earth's age.

workedExamples.title: Evaluating a theory
workedExamples.question: Scientists measure the gases released by volcanoes today and find they are mostly water vapour and carbon dioxide, with some nitrogen. Explain how this evidence supports the theory of the early atmosphere.
steps: The theory says the early atmosphere came from volcanic gases.
Modern volcanic gases contain the same gases the theory predicts: water vapour (which could form oceans), carbon dioxide (the main gas) and nitrogen.
Limitation: modern volcanoes may not release exactly the same mixture as volcanoes 4 billion years ago, so the evidence is supporting but not proof.
workedExamples.answer: The gases match those the theory predicts, so the evidence supports the theory, but it is indirect evidence.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think the early atmosphere contained lots of oxygen, because we need oxygen to live.
misconceptions.right: In fact it had little or no oxygen. Oxygen built up much later because of photosynthesis by algae and plants.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think scientists know exactly what the early atmosphere contained.
misconceptions.right: In fact evidence is limited because of the 4.6 billion year time scale, so scientists use theories that change as new evidence appears.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think the oceans have always existed.
misconceptions.right: In fact one theory says water vapour from volcanoes condensed to form the oceans as the Earth cooled.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think carbon dioxide was removed only by plants.
misconceptions.right: In fact carbon dioxide first decreased when it dissolved in the newly formed oceans and carbonates were precipitated as sediments.

realWorld: Space probes measuring the atmospheres of Mars and Venus provide evidence that rocky planets without life have atmospheres that are mainly carbon dioxide.
Volcanologists sample gases from active volcanoes, such as those in Iceland and Hawaii, which are mostly water vapour and carbon dioxide.
Very old rocks and sediments are analysed to look for chemical clues about conditions on the early Earth.
examTips: Use the AQA key points in order: volcanoes, gases released, mainly carbon dioxide, little or no oxygen, water vapour condensed to form oceans, nitrogen built up.
Say 'little or no oxygen', not just 'no oxygen'; both words matter for full marks in describe questions.
When evaluating evidence, mention that evidence is limited because the Earth is 4.6 billion years old, and that a theory can change with new evidence.
Do not mix up the stages: carbon dioxide dissolving in oceans and forming carbonate sediments is part of this topic; photosynthesis comes later.
summary: The Earth is about 4.6 billion years old, so evidence about the early atmosphere is limited.
Intense volcanic activity in the first billion years released the gases of the early atmosphere.
The early atmosphere was mainly carbon dioxide with little or no oxygen, like Mars and Venus today.
Water vapour condensed to form the oceans.
Nitrogen gradually built up; small amounts of methane and ammonia may have been present.
Carbon dioxide dissolved in the oceans and carbonates precipitated as sediments.

questions.question: What was the main gas in the Earth's early atmosphere, according to the theory in this topic?
markScheme: 1 mark: carbon dioxide
questions.explanation: The early atmosphere was probably mainly carbon dioxide, like Mars and Venus today. Nitrogen is the main gas today, and oxygen came much later.

questions.question: What was the main source of the gases in the Earth's early atmosphere?
markScheme: 1 mark: volcanic activity
questions.explanation: Intense volcanic activity released gases. Photosynthesis and animals came much later, and fossil fuels formed much later still.

questions.question: How much oxygen was in the Earth's early atmosphere?
markScheme: 1 mark: little or none
questions.explanation: There was little or no oxygen. Oxygen built up after algae and plants began photosynthesis.

questions.question: How did the oceans form?
options: Water vapour from volcanoes condensed as the Earth cooled.
Ice from space melted when it reached the Earth.
Oxygen and hydrogen reacted in the air.
Rain fell from clouds of methane.
markScheme: 1 mark: water vapour from volcanoes condensed
questions.explanation: AQA's theory is that volcanoes released water vapour, which condensed to form the oceans as the Earth cooled.

questions.question: The Earth's early atmosphere may have been like the atmospheres of which two planets today?
markScheme: 1 mark: Mars and Venus
questions.explanation: Mars and Venus are rocky planets with atmospheres that are mainly carbon dioxide with little or no oxygen.

questions.question: Which gas produced by volcanoes gradually built up in the early atmosphere and is still the main gas today?
markScheme: 1 mark: nitrogen
questions.explanation: Nitrogen is unreactive, so once released by volcanoes it gradually built up. It is now about four-fifths of the air.

questions.question: Which pair of gases may have been present in small proportions in the early atmosphere?
markScheme: 1 mark: methane and ammonia
questions.explanation: AQA states there may have been small proportions of methane and ammonia. There was little or no oxygen, so oxygen and ozone are wrong.

questions.question: Why is the evidence about the Earth's early atmosphere limited?
options: Scientists have not been allowed to study it.
The Earth is about 4.6 billion years old, so little direct evidence remains.
All rocks from the early Earth are radioactive.
markScheme: 1 mark: time scale of 4.6 billion years
questions.explanation: The very long time scale means there were no direct measurements and few unchanged rocks survive.

questions.question: What happened when carbon dioxide dissolved in the early oceans?
markScheme: 1 mark: carbonates precipitated forming sediments
questions.explanation: Dissolved carbon dioxide led to carbonates precipitating, producing sediments. This reduced the carbon dioxide in the atmosphere. It did not form oxygen; that needed photosynthesis.

questions.question: Which observation would provide the strongest support for the theory that the early atmosphere came from volcanoes?
options: The Earth's atmosphere today is mostly nitrogen.
Gases from volcanoes today are mostly water vapour and carbon dioxide, with some nitrogen.
markScheme: 1 mark: modern volcanic gases are mostly water vapour and carbon dioxide with some nitrogen
questions.explanation: If modern volcanic gases match the gases the theory predicts, this supports the idea. The other statements are true but do not test where the early gases came from.

questions.question: A scientist finds very old rocks containing iron compounds that only form when there is little or no oxygen. What does this evidence suggest?
options: The early atmosphere had a high percentage of oxygen.
The early atmosphere had little or no oxygen.
There were no volcanoes on the early Earth.
The oceans formed before the Earth cooled.
markScheme: 1 mark: the early atmosphere had little or no oxygen
questions.explanation: If these compounds only form without oxygen, finding them in old rocks suggests that there was little or no oxygen at the time, which supports the theory.

questions.question: The Earth is about 4.6 billion years old. Write 4.6 billion as an ordinary number (1 billion = 1 000 000 000).
questions.explanation: 4.6 × 1 000 000 000 = 4 600 000 000 years, or 4.6 × 10⁹ years in standard form.

questions.question: Intense volcanic activity is thought to have happened during the first billion years of the Earth's 4.6 billion year history. Calculate this as a percentage of the Earth's age. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.
markScheme: 1 mark: 22%
questions.explanation: 1 ÷ 4.6 = 0.2174, × 100 = 21.7%, which is 22% to 2 significant figures.

questions.question:
Example data: a 200 cm³ sample of gas collected from a volcano contains 30 cm³ of carbon dioxide.
Calculate the percentage of carbon dioxide in the sample.
markScheme: 1 mark: 15%

questions.question: The atmosphere of Mars is about 95% carbon dioxide. Calculate the volume of carbon dioxide in a 250 cm³ sample of Martian atmosphere.
markScheme: 1 mark: 237.5 cm³ (accept 238 cm³)

questions.question: The atmosphere of Venus is about 96% carbon dioxide and the Earth's atmosphere today is about 0.04% carbon dioxide. Calculate how many times greater the percentage of carbon dioxide is on Venus.
markScheme: 1 mark: 2400
questions.explanation: 96 ÷ 0.04 = 2400. Dividing by a small decimal gives a large number: 0.04 goes into 1 twenty-five times, so into 96 it goes 96 × 25 = 2400 times.

questions.question: Name the process that released the gases that formed the Earth's early atmosphere.
markScheme: 1 mark: volcanic activity / volcanoes erupting
questions.explanation: Intense volcanic activity during the first billion years released the gases.

questions.question: Give one way the Earth's early atmosphere was different from the atmosphere today.
markScheme: 1 mark: much more carbon dioxide / mainly carbon dioxide OR little or no oxygen OR less nitrogen
questions.explanation: The early atmosphere was mainly carbon dioxide with little or no oxygen. Today it is mainly nitrogen and oxygen with very little carbon dioxide.

questions.question: Describe how the oceans formed, according to the theory in this topic.
markScheme: 1 mark: volcanoes released water vapour
1 mark: (as the Earth cooled) the water vapour condensed to form the oceans
questions.explanation: Two linked ideas are needed: the source of the water (volcanic water vapour) and the change of state (condensing).

questions.question: Explain how the formation of the oceans reduced the amount of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere.
acceptedAnswers: carbon dioxide dissolved in the oceans
markScheme: 1 mark: carbon dioxide dissolved in the ocean water
1 mark: carbonates were precipitated, producing sediments (so carbon was removed from the air)
questions.explanation: Carbon dioxide is soluble in water. Once dissolved, carbonates precipitated as sediments, locking the carbon away on the sea bed.

questions.question: Explain why scientists cannot be certain about the composition of the Earth's early atmosphere.
markScheme: 1 mark: the time scale is very long (about 4.6 billion years)
1 mark: so evidence is limited / indirect / no one could measure it
questions.explanation: The answer needs both the reason (time scale) and the consequence (limited evidence).

questions.question: Name two gases that may have been present in small proportions in the early atmosphere, and give the formula of each.
markScheme: 1 mark: methane, CH₄
1 mark: ammonia, NH₃
questions.explanation: Methane is CH₄ and ammonia is NH₃. Both may have been present in small proportions.

questions.question: Nitrogen gradually built up in the atmosphere while carbon dioxide decreased. Suggest why nitrogen built up rather than being removed.
markScheme: 1 mark: nitrogen is unreactive / does not dissolve much in water
1 mark: so it was not removed by dissolving or reactions, and kept accumulating as volcanoes released more
questions.explanation: Carbon dioxide was removed by dissolving and later by photosynthesis. Nitrogen is very unreactive, so it was not removed and accumulated over time.

questions.question: Venus and Mars have atmospheres that are mainly carbon dioxide. Explain how this information is used as evidence for the theory of the Earth's early atmosphere, and give one limitation of this evidence.
markScheme: 1 mark: Mars and Venus are rocky planets that formed in a similar way / have had volcanic activity
1 mark: they have no life (no photosynthesis), so their atmospheres may show what the Earth's was like before life changed it
1 mark: limitation: conditions on these planets differ from the Earth (for example temperature, size, distance from the Sun), so the comparison is indirect
questions.explanation: Comparisons with similar planets are a type of indirect evidence: useful, but not proof, because the planets are not identical to the early Earth.

questions.question: Scientists' theories about the early atmosphere have changed over time. Suggest why theories change.
markScheme: 1 mark: new evidence is found / new techniques for analysing rocks or planets
1 mark: theories are modified to fit all the evidence (after being checked by other scientists)
questions.explanation: Scientific theories are revised when new evidence appears that the old theory cannot explain.

questions.question: Describe the theory of how the Earth's early atmosphere and oceans formed during the first billion years of the Earth's existence.
markScheme: Indicative content: intense volcanic activity; volcanoes released gases; mainly carbon dioxide; little or no oxygen; like Mars and Venus today; water vapour released; condensed as Earth cooled to form oceans; nitrogen released and gradually built up; small proportions of methane and ammonia possible.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): a clear description linking volcanoes, carbon dioxide-rich atmosphere with little or no oxygen, and condensation of water vapour to form oceans.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements, for example 'volcanoes made the atmosphere' or 'there was lots of carbon dioxide'.
questions.explanation: Cover both the atmosphere (gases and their source) and the oceans (condensing water vapour) to reach Level 2.

questions.question: Describe the theory of how the Earth's early atmosphere formed and how the amount of carbon dioxide first began to decrease. Evaluate the evidence that supports this theory.
markScheme: Indicative content: first billion years; intense volcanic activity; released mainly carbon dioxide, water vapour, nitrogen, possibly small amounts of methane and ammonia; little or no oxygen; similar to Mars and Venus; water vapour condensed to form oceans; carbon dioxide dissolved in oceans; carbonates precipitated forming sediments, reducing atmospheric carbon dioxide. Evaluation: supporting evidence includes gases from volcanoes today, atmospheres of Mars and Venus, carbonate sedimentary rocks; but evidence is limited because of the 4.6 billion year time scale; much is indirect; conditions on other planets and modern volcanoes may differ; theories may change with new evidence.
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): a detailed, logically ordered description of formation and carbon dioxide removal, with a balanced evaluation of evidence including at least one limitation.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): a description of formation with some reference to carbon dioxide dissolving, and some comment on evidence.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): basic statements about volcanoes or carbon dioxide with little or no evaluation.
questions.explanation: Evaluation means weighing up: give evidence for the theory and explain why it is not certain (time scale, indirect evidence).
